set1.q: A 64-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven 2.8-cm non-small cell carcinoma in the right upper lobe. Positron emission tomography shows uptake in a hilar lymph node on the same side, but no mediastinal or other nodes are involved, and there is no distant metastasis. Which stage is her cancer?
opts: Stage 1A is a tumor no more than 3 cm with no lymph node spread. Tell: her tumor size fits stage 1A, but the involved hilar node rules out any stage that requires clear nodes.
Stage 2A is a tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm with no lymph node spread. Tell: her tumor is smaller than that and her hilar node is involved, which is the other route into stage 2B.

Correct. A tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes is stage 2B. Her 2.8-cm tumor would be stage 1A without nodes, but the involved same-side hilar node, scored N1, moves it to stage 2B; mediastinal nodes would have made it stage 3.

Stage 3A with a small tumor needs spread to the mediastinal or subcarinal nodes, because N2 or N3 involvement moves a cancer to stage 3. Tell: her involved node is hilar on the same side, N1, which stops at stage 2B.

opts: Biopsy classes the type of tumor, which hers already has as adenocarcinoma. Tell: lymph node involvement in staging is assessed by positron emission tomography, while computed tomography gives size and location.

Pulmonary function tests are part of the additional workup and measure how well the lungs work. Tell: they do not image the lymph nodes; positron emission tomography looks at lymph involvement, and computed tomography gives size and location.
A chest film is not a good tool here; at most it first shows a nodule or rules out other pathology. Tell: node involvement for staging comes from positron emission tomography.

Correct. Lung cancer is staged once computed tomography, positron emission tomography and biopsy results are back: computed tomography identifies location and size, positron emission tomography looks at lymph involvement, and biopsy classes the tumor type. Tumor size, node involvement and distant metastasis then set the stage.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man with a 50 pack-year history is diagnosed with small cell lung carcinoma after presenting with bone pain. Computed tomography shows a mass beside the left hilum. His wife asks where this cancer usually arises and why it was not caught earlier. Which response is accurate?
opts: Correct. Small cell carcinoma has a central location and infiltrates the mucosa, so it develops insidiously, and over 70% of patients are metastatic, to the liver, bone or brain, before detection. His hilar mass and bone pain fit that pattern: central, and already spread when found.

Peripheral location belongs to adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma, and even those are not amenable to early detection. Tell: small cell carcinoma is central, beside the hilum as in his scan, and is usually metastatic when found.

The location is right but the behavior is reversed: small cell carcinoma develops insidiously, and over 70% of patients are metastatic before detection. Tell: his presenting complaint was bone pain, a sign that spread had already happened.

Sputum testing catches squamous cell carcinoma, a central bronchial tumor, while peripheral tumors are the hardest to detect early. Tell: small cell carcinoma is central, and its problem is early, silent metastasis.

set1.q: A 63-year-old woman who still smokes and has a 50 pack-year history has had 6 weeks of hemoptysis and has lost 4 kg. She saw an advertisement and asks to enroll in a lung cancer screening program. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Correct. Screening is for high-risk individuals without symptoms or a known nodule. Hemoptysis and weight loss are symptoms that should be worked up for possible lung cancer now, with computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen followed by biopsy, so screening would delay her diagnosis.

Computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen is the standard study for symptoms of possible lung cancer. Tell: she needs exactly this diagnostic scan, so it is not the plan to avoid.

Biopsy follows the contrast scan in the standard workup, by bronchoscopy, a transthoracic approach or thoracoscopy depending on location. Tell: tissue diagnosis is a needed step for a symptomatic patient, not one to avoid.

A comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium is part of the laboratory workup, beside a complete blood count with differential and alkaline phosphatase. Tell: these laboratory studies support her diagnostic workup and are appropriate.

set1.q: A 72-year-old woman with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an image-guided biopsy confirming non-small cell carcinoma in a 1.8-cm peripheral nodule, with no lymph node or distant spread. Her surgeon judges her fit for an operation, but her pulmonary function tests show she would not tolerate losing a whole lobe. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. When a fit patient's image-guided biopsy confirms malignancy, the options are lobectomy or, if the patient is unfit for lobectomy, an anatomical segmentectomy. A segment resection removes a larger portion of the lobe than a wedge but less than a lobectomy, and the operation must be one she can survive and recover from.

Lobectomy removes the entire lobe and is the standard resection when a patient can tolerate it. Tell: her pulmonary function shows she would not tolerate losing a whole lobe, so the pathway turns to anatomical segmentectomy instead.
ruled out by a stated finding

Pneumonectomy removes the entire lung, even more tissue than a lobectomy. Tell: she cannot tolerate losing a whole lobe, so removing the whole lung is further out of reach; a patient must be able to survive and recover from surgery.
ruled out by a stated finding

For non-small cell cancer, chemotherapy and radiation are adjuncts to surgery or the approach in stage 4, because these tumors respond poorly to them. Tell: her tumor is small with no nodal or distant spread, and she is fit for a limited operation.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man who smokes has a bronchial biopsy showing dysplasia: the cells have changed form but have not invaded the surrounding tissue. He asks what would come next if these cells keep progressing. Which change comes next?
opts: Correct. Lung cancer develops in a sequence: a genetically altered epithelial cell, hyperplasia (cells dividing faster than normal), dysplasia (cells changing form), in situ cancer (cells staying in one place), then a malignant tumor whose cells invade normal tissue and enter blood and lymph, and finally distant metastases. After dysplasia comes in situ cancer.

Hyperplasia, cells dividing more rapidly than normal, comes before dysplasia in the sequence, not after it. Tell: his cells have already changed form, which is dysplasia, so the next stage is in situ cancer, cells that stay in one place.

Invasion of normal tissue with entry into blood and lymph marks a malignant tumor, which follows in situ cancer rather than dysplasia directly. Tell: in situ cancer, cells that stay in one place, sits between dysplasia and invasion.

Metastases at distant sites are the last stage of the sequence, after in situ cancer and invasion into blood and lymph. Tell: his biopsy shows dysplasia without invasion, so two stages still separate him from distant spread.

set1.q: A 71-year-old man who still smokes and has a 60 pack-year history has a new, solid 22-mm nodule in the left upper lobe with a spiculated (spiky) border. His primary care clinician judges the probability of malignancy to be high. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Hospice skips the whole pathway: no staging has been done, and if no metastases are found the plan is resection. Tell: a high-probability nodule is staged and referred to a subspecialist for removal, not moved straight to end-of-life care.

Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Tell: he already has a suspicious nodule, so the next move is diagnostic staging and subspecialist referral, not enrollment in yearly screening scans.

Quitting smoking is worthwhile, but it does not address a nodule already judged high probability for malignancy. Tell: the recommended referral for a high-probability nodule is a subspecialist such as a thoracic surgeon, pulmonologist, interventional radiologist or oncologist.

Correct. A high probability of malignancy in a new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm leads to standard stage evaluation and, when no metastases are found, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection, and referral to a subspecialist such as a thoracic surgeon is recommended. His upper-lobe location, spiky border and heavy smoking all add to the concern.

set1.q: An 81-year-old woman with severe heart failure is unfit for surgery. Computed tomography shows a growing 2.5-cm nodule lying against a large blood vessel, and the interventional radiologist judges image-guided biopsy unsafe. Positron emission tomography shows intense uptake in the nodule and no lymph node or distant spread. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Biopsy is done in unfit patients when it is possible and safe. Tell: her radiologist judged it unsafe, and the pathway allows treatment without tissue in exactly that situation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Wedge resection with frozen section is a surgical route for fit patients. Tell: she is unfit for surgery because of severe heart failure, so resection of any size is off the table.
ruled out by a stated finding

Waiting a year leaves a growing, intensely avid nodule untreated in a patient who still has a nonsurgical option. Tell: when biopsy is unsafe in an unfit patient, the pathway proceeds directly to stereotactic ablative or conventional radical radiotherapy, or radiofrequency ablation.

Correct. For a patient unfit for surgery, image-guided biopsy is the next step only if it is possible and safe. When biopsy is not possible or not safe, the pathway goes straight to stereotactic ablative radiotherapy, radiofrequency ablation or conventional radical radiotherapy, so her unsafe biopsy does not block treatment.

set1.q: A 59-year-old woman with limited-stage small cell lung carcinoma has a complete response to initial chemotherapy and thoracic radiation. Her cognition is normal and she is active and independent. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Observation alone skips the adjuvant step recommended for limited-stage disease after a complete or partial response. Tell: brain metastasis is so likely in small cell carcinoma that the brain is radiated prophylactically.

Lobectomy is a resection used for non-small cell cancer, which responds poorly to chemotherapy and radiation. Tell: her small cell cancer has already responded completely to chemotherapy and radiation, and the next step is prophylactic cranial irradiation.

Positron emission tomography is not recommended for routine follow-up after small cell treatment. Tell: after a complete response in limited stage, the adjuvant step is prophylactic cranial irradiation.

Correct. After initial therapy, limited-stage small cell carcinoma with a complete or partial response goes on to prophylactic cranial irradiation, radiating the brain to prevent metastasis because brain spread is so likely. Her normal cognition and good function leave no reason to withhold it.

set1.q: A 65-year-old woman with a biopsy-proven 4-cm non-small cell carcinoma has a staging scan showing metastases in the right adrenal gland and in several vertebrae. Which stage is her cancer?
opts: Stage 3B rests on lymph node spread, such as supraclavicular or scalene nodes with a smaller tumor, without metastasis. Tell: adrenal and bone lesions are distant metastases, which place her in stage 4.

Stage 3C is a tumor larger than 5 cm with spread to supraclavicular or scalene nodes or the far side's nodes, but no metastasis. Tell: her adrenal and bone lesions are distant spread, and every stage 1 to 3 cancer is M0.

Stage 4A allows spread within the chest to the other lung, pleura, pericardium or surrounding fluid, or to just one site outside the chest, such as one adrenal gland. Tell: she has two sites outside the chest, adrenal and bone, which is stage 4B.

Correct. Multiple extrathoracic metastases, in one or more organs, are scored M1c, and spread to multiple sites outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland and bones, is stage 4B. Any tumor size and any node status still give stage 4B once the cancer has reached several sites beyond the chest.

set1.q: A 62-year-old woman with a 35 pack-year smoking history is diagnosed with lung cancer. She asks how cigarette smoke turned normal lung cells into cancer. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Correct. Carcinogens, or other causes of genetic mutation, activate oncogenes in lung cells, and further mutations or loss of regulatory control inactivate tumor suppressor genes. Atypical cells then proliferate locally and spread, becoming poorly differentiated as the cancer grows and drives angiogenesis to exceed its boundaries.

This reverses both switches: carcinogens activate oncogenes, and further mutations inactivate the tumor suppressor genes that normally restrain growth. Tell: cancer needs the growth signals turned on and the brakes turned off, the opposite of this option.

Growing lung cancer cells become poorly differentiated and transition from epithelial to other cell types, rather than maturing. Tell: loss of differentiation is part of how the cancer spreads, so more differentiation runs the wrong way.

Tuberculosis and human immunodeficiency virus infection are listed as separate risk factors, but carcinogens in smoke act through genetic mutation, not infection. Tell: smoke activates oncogenes and inactivates tumor suppressor genes in the lung cells themselves.

set1.q: A 67-year-old man with lung adenocarcinoma has metastases in the liver, an adrenal gland and several bones, placing him at stage 4B. Which treatment is standard for his cancer?
opts: Correct. For non-small cell lung cancer, stage 4 is treated with chemotherapy, with surgical resection considered only for a solitary metastatic lesion with a resectable primary tumor. Chemotherapy and radiation are used as adjuncts to surgery or when the patient is stage 4. He has metastases at several sites, so resection is not the plan.

Lobectomy belongs to earlier stages, where surgical resection is the standard for stage 1 and 2 disease. Tell: with metastases in the liver, adrenal gland and bones, removing the primary lobe cannot treat his disease.

Pneumonectomy, removal of the entire lung, is a resection chosen by size and lymph involvement in operable disease. Tell: in stage 4, resection is considered only for a single metastatic lesion with a resectable primary, and he has several.
Observation leaves treatable disease untreated: stage 4 non-small cell lung cancer still has a standard therapy. Tell: standard management for stage 4 is chemotherapy, not watchful waiting.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman has a biopsy-proven large cell carcinoma in the periphery of the right lung. Her oncologist warns that this tumor type can spread to a site that is unusual for lung cancers. Which site is it?
opts: Bone, including the spine, is a usual metastatic site for lung cancer, causing pain, fractures and cord compression. Tell: large cell carcinoma stands out for spreading to the small intestine and bowel.

Correct. Large cell carcinoma metastasizes to rare areas such as the small intestine and bowel, a pattern specific to this tumor type. Lung cancers in general spread to regional lymph nodes and then to the liver, brain and bone, so those sites are expected rather than unusual.
The liver is one of the usual distant sites for lung cancer, beside the brain and bone. Tell: the question asks for the unusual site tied to large cell carcinoma, the small intestine and bowel.

The brain is a common metastatic site for lung cancers, causing headaches, vision changes and seizures. Tell: it is expected rather than unusual; large cell carcinoma's unusual site is the small intestine and bowel.

set1.q: A 66-year-old man with a 60 pack-year history is brought to the emergency department with new confusion, an unsteady gait and a seizure. Serum sodium is 118 mEq/L (normal 135-145) and serum osmolality is 250 mOsm/kg (normal 275-295). He has no peripheral edema and no signs of pulmonary edema. Computed tomography shows a central hilar mass. Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Adenocarcinoma usually forms in the mid-lung and periphery, and its later signs are bone pain, weight loss and other systemic issues. Tell: a central hilar mass with inappropriate antidiuretic hormone points to small cell carcinoma.

A bronchial carcinoid causes carcinoid syndrome from serotonin release: flushing, diarrhea, wheezing and right-sided valve thickening. Tell: his problem is water retention with low sodium and osmolality, the antidiuretic hormone syndrome of small cell carcinoma.

Correct. Small cell lung cancer can produce the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone through its neuroendocrine cells, causing excess vasopressin and water retention. The result is hyponatremia and low serum osmolality, here 118 and 250, with confusion, seizures and ataxia but no peripheral or pulmonary edema, because the process is insidious. The central mass fits too.

Squamous cell carcinoma is also central, but its particular paraneoplastic finding is hypercalcemia. Tell: very low sodium and osmolality with neurologic symptoms and no edema is inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, the small cell syndrome.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man who smokes 2 packs a day is worried after his brother was diagnosed with lung cancer. He asks which type of lung cancer is most strongly associated with smoking. Which response is accurate?
opts: A bronchial carcinoid is a rare type, known for carcinoid syndrome from serotonin release. Tell: the cancer singled out for the strongest association with smoking is squamous cell carcinoma.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma, the second most common lung cancer, has the strongest association with smoking. Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of all lung cancers and compounds with packs per day and years, but among the cell types it is squamous cell carcinoma that is singled out as most strongly tied to smoking.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer, and smoking is not always associated with it; it also occurs in people who never smoked. Tell: the strongest smoking link belongs to squamous cell carcinoma.

Large cell carcinoma is a peripheral non-small cell cancer known for unusual metastases to the small intestine and bowel. Tell: it is not the type singled out for the strongest smoking association; squamous cell carcinoma is.

opts: Hemoptysis and fatigue are listed among the early respiratory presentations of adenocarcinoma. Tell: the later signs are systemic, bone pain and weight loss, as the cancer spreads.
Metastasis to the small intestine and bowel is the unusual pattern of large cell carcinoma. Tell: his tumor is adenocarcinoma, whose later signs are bone pain, weight loss and other systemic issues.

Correct. Adenocarcinoma is mostly asymptomatic early and usually presents first with respiratory symptoms: cough, shortness of breath, chest tightness or pain, hemoptysis and fatigue. Later signs are bone pain, weight loss and other systemic, paraneoplastic issues, and two thirds of patients present only once the disease is advanced or metastatic.

Cough and chest tightness are the early respiratory symptoms that usually come first. Tell: these brought him to diagnosis; later disease shows itself with bone pain, weight loss and other systemic issues.

set1.q: A 59-year-old man with active pulmonary sarcoidosis and a 30 pack-year history has a new 16-mm solid nodule. Positron emission tomography shows high uptake in the nodule. He asks whether this result proves he has cancer. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Dismissing the uptake as inflammation is as unsafe as calling it cancer: highly metabolic cells take up the sugar, suggesting malignancy. Tell: inflammation is a possible explanation, not a proven one, so the nodule needs a biopsy.
Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Tell: he already has a nodule with high uptake, so he needs diagnostic tissue sampling rather than yearly screening.

Correct. Positron emission tomography uses a radioactive sugar that highly metabolic cells take up, suggesting malignancy, but high uptake does not rule out inflammatory conditions, which may also take it up. With an active inflammatory lung disease his uptake cannot prove cancer, so tissue is needed; moderate or intense uptake leads to biopsy or resection.

Treating before tissue confirms cancer assumes the scan is proof, yet inflammatory conditions may also show high uptake. Tell: uptake raises suspicion and a biopsy decides it; chemotherapy for non-small cell cancer is an adjunct or stage 4 therapy anyway.

set1.q: A 66-year-old woman with a 40 pack-year history has a new, solid 18-mm nodule. Her clinician judged the probability of malignancy low to moderate, and positron emission tomography now shows intense uptake in the nodule. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule; it is not how a found nodule is managed. Tell: she already has a nodule with intense uptake, so she needs a diagnostic biopsy, not entry into a screening program.

Repeating the scan adds nothing to the decision: intense uptake already places her on the biopsy or resection branch. Tell: uptake raises suspicion but cannot by itself separate cancer from inflammation, which may also take up the tracer, so tissue is needed.

Correct. Moderate or intense uptake on fludeoxyglucose positron emission tomography moves a low-to-moderate probability nodule to nonsurgical biopsy, by transthoracic needle or endoscopic approach, or to video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection, with referral to a subspecialist such as a pulmonologist, thoracic surgeon, interventional radiologist or oncologist.

Serial surveillance scans at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months follow negative or mild uptake, or a very low probability. Tell: her nodule showed intense uptake, which suggests highly metabolic cells and calls for tissue rather than watching.

set1.q: A 64-year-old woman with a 40 pack-year history is diagnosed with metastatic lung cancer after presenting with bone pain and weight loss. She never had a cough. Her son asks why the cancer was not found until it had spread. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Screening's documented downside is the opposite problem: a high rate of false positives that turn out benign, while its upside is early detection that improves prognosis. Tell: late diagnosis comes from silent growth, and screening applies to eligible high-risk people without symptoms.

Correct. What makes lung cancer so deadly is that patients usually have no symptoms until the disease is advanced or already metastatic. Patients may have no respiratory symptoms at all and present instead with complaints from metastasis, such as bone pain, so her bone pain and weight loss were late signs of silent growth.
Most tumors start in the periphery

Most lung cancers form a mass in or near the hilum; only some form in the periphery, where they are difficult to diagnose. Tell: the main reason for late diagnosis is that symptoms appear only when the disease is advanced or metastatic, not a mostly peripheral origin.

Spread before symptoms is common: over 70% of small cell carcinomas are metastatic before detection, and two thirds of adenocarcinomas present advanced or metastatic. Tell: her first symptoms came from bone metastasis, which is exactly this silent spread.

set1.q: A 36-year-old woman who has never smoked has had a persistent cough for 3 months and has now coughed up blood twice. A chest film shows a 3-cm mass. A friend told her that lung cancer does not happen at her age. Which response is accurate?
opts: This reverses the age pattern: most lung cancers occur in people older than 50, with about 4% under 40. Tell: her age makes lung cancer less likely, not more, yet her symptoms still call for a workup.

Correct. Most lung cancers occur in people older than 50, but about 4% occur in people under 40, so her age does not remove it from the differential. Persistent cough and hemoptysis are symptoms that should be worked up for possible lung cancer, and smoking, though implicated in 85 to 90% of cases, is not required.

About 4% of lung cancers occur in people under 40, so her age lowers the likelihood without excluding the disease. Tell: a symptomatic young patient with persistent cough, hemoptysis and a mass still needs a workup for possible lung cancer.

Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of cases, not every case; radon, radiation, air pollution, toxins and genetics are other listed risk factors. Tell: never having smoked lowers her risk but does not rule out lung cancer in a symptomatic patient with a mass.

set1.q: A 58-year-old man who quit smoking 30 years ago has an 8-mm nodule on computed tomography done for a rib fracture. It is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with dense calcification in its center and no fat. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: A linear scar or lymphoid tissue appears as a nodular opacity next to the minor fissure. Tell: his finding is a rounded solid nodule with central calcification, the picture of a healed granuloma.

Correct. A smoothly marginated solid nodule with central calcification is typical of a healed granuloma, an inflammatory nodule and one of the main examples of benign nodules. Central calcification is a benign pattern, whereas eccentric or stippled ground-glass calcification is a malignant pattern.
A hamartoma is a smoothly marginated nodule with internal fat and calcification, classically popcorn-looking. Tell: his nodule has central calcification and no fat, the healed granuloma pattern.

Squamous cell carcinoma is a central bronchial tumor, often large and cavitated with a spiky border. Tell: a small, smooth nodule with centrally placed calcification shows a benign pattern rather than malignant features.

opts: Small cells that lack nucleoli, with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasm ratio in crushed, fragile tissue, describe small cell carcinoma. Tell: her biopsy already shows a non-small cell carcinoma, and adenocarcinoma is supported by mucin.

Large, anaplastic, undifferentiated cells about three times normal size describe large cell carcinoma, a diagnosis of exclusion. Tell: adenocarcinoma is identified by mucin production on a mucicarmine stain, not by anaplastic cells.

Correct. Histology may include a mucicarmine stain: mucin production is related to adenocarcinoma, while negative staining may point to large cell carcinoma. A negative mucicarmine stain may point to large cell carcinoma, the non-small cell type with no specific markers. Tell: adenocarcinoma is the mucin producer, so a positive stain, not a negative one, supports it.

opts: Serial surveillance scans fit a very low probability or negative to mild uptake on positron emission tomography. Tell: a high-probability nodule goes to staging and then resection, because watching it would delay treatment of a likely cancer.
Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Tell: she already has a suspicious nodule, so she needs diagnostic staging, not a yearly screening scan.

A chest film is not a good tool for working up a nodule, beyond first showing it or ruling out other pathology. Tell: a high-probability nodule moves on to staging and resection, not back to plain films.

If no metastases are identified, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection follows. Her upper-lobe location, spiky border and heavy smoking support the high estimate.

set1.q: A 67-year-old man with small cell lung carcinoma diagnosed 2 months ago has a dull ache under his right ribs, poor appetite and yellowing of his eyes. Exam shows an enlarged liver with a firm edge. Which complication has developed?
opts: Bone metastasis causes bone pain, fractures without falls and spinal cord compression. Tell: his complaints are a right upper quadrant ache, jaundice and a firm enlarged liver, which localize the spread to the liver.

Brain metastasis presents with headaches, vision changes, vomiting, syncope or seizures and papilledema. Tell: jaundice and a firm enlarged liver are hepatic findings, and he has no neurologic complaints.

Adrenal metastasis causes adrenal insufficiency with fatigue, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Tell: yellowing of the eyes and a firm, enlarged liver point to liver involvement instead.

Correct. Small cell carcinoma is metastatic, to the liver, bone or brain, before detection in over 70% of patients. Liver metastasis causes a dull right upper quadrant ache, hepatomegaly with a firm edge, lack of appetite, jaundice and eventually hepatic failure, matching his findings.

set1.q: A 64-year-old man with a 50 pack-year history has a central lung mass, and biopsy shows small cell carcinoma. Over 2 months he has developed progressive muscle weakness, worst in his legs. Testing confirms Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (autoimmune muscle weakness, particularly in the legs). He asks what causes the weakness. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Low sodium from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone causes confusion, seizures and ataxia. Tell: his diagnosis is an antibody attack on calcium channels at nerve endings, not an electrolyte effect.

The antibodies target the nerve side of the neuromuscular junction, not the muscle fibers themselves. Tell: calcium channels on the nerve endings stop working, too little acetylcholine is released, and the muscles cannot contract properly.

Correct. Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is a rare autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks calcium channels on nerve endings at the neuromuscular junction. The non-functioning channels prevent release of acetylcholine, so the muscles cannot contract properly, producing progressive weakness, particularly in the legs.

Spinal cord compression comes from bone metastasis to the spine. Tell: his weakness has an autoimmune cause at the neuromuscular junction, where antibodies disable calcium channels on nerve endings and too little acetylcholine is released.

opts: An optional scan at 12 months is the entry for a nodule smaller than 6 mm in a high-risk patient. Tell: he is low risk with a 7-mm nodule, which calls for a scan at 6 to 12 months.
Considering a scan at 3 months, positron emission tomography or tissue sampling applies to single nodules larger than 8 mm. Tell: his nodule is 7 mm, so he follows the 6-to-8-mm schedule instead.

Correct. For a single solid nodule of 6 to 8 mm in a low-risk patient, the Fleischner Society table gives computed tomography at 6 to 12 months, then considering another scan at 18 to 24 months. He has never smoked and has no other risk factors, so he is low risk.

A scan at 6 to 12 months is the schedule for a single nodule of 6 to 8 mm. Tell: she has two nodules, and multiple nodules of this size in a high-risk patient are rescanned sooner, at 3 to 6 months.

set1.q: A 72-year-old man has a biopsy-proven 3.6-cm non-small cell carcinoma in the left lower lobe. Staging shows no lymph node involvement and no distant metastasis. Which stage is his cancer?
opts: Stage 1A is a tumor no more than 3 cm in its greatest dimension with no lymph node spread. Tell: his tumor measures 3.6 cm, past the 3-cm limit, which moves it up to stage 1B even though his nodes are clear.

Correct. A tumor more than 3 cm but no more than 4 cm in its greatest dimension, with no lymph node spread and no metastasis, is stage 1B. His 3.6-cm tumor with clear nodes sits in that band; at this stage the tumor may or may not involve the main bronchus or the lung's inner lining.
Stage 2A is a tumor more than 4 cm but no more than 5 cm with no lymph node spread. Tell: his 3.6-cm tumor has not reached 4 cm, so with clear nodes and no metastasis it remains stage 1B.

Stage 3A needs a tumor larger than 7 cm or one invading structures such as the diaphragm or mediastinum, or spread to mediastinal or subcarinal nodes. Tell: he has a 3.6-cm tumor with clear nodes, none of those.

Weeks later he develops crampy abdominal pain, and imaging shows a metastasis in the small intestine. Biopsy of the lung mass shows undifferentiated cells about three times normal size that do not stain for mucin. Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Correct. Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery, shows a large cavitated mass on computed tomography, and has anaplastic, undifferentiated cells about 3 times larger than baseline that lack specific markers. Negative mucicarmine staining may point to it, and its spread to unusual sites such as the small intestine and bowel is characteristic.

Adenocarcinoma is also peripheral, but it produces mucin, shown on a mucicarmine stain. Tell: his tumor cells are mucin-negative, very large and undifferentiated, and the cancer has reached the small intestine, an unusual site typical of large cell carcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma cavitates too, but it sits centrally and often arises in a bronchus. Tell: his mass is peripheral and has spread to the small intestine, a pattern specific to large cell carcinoma.
Small cell carcinoma is central, with small cells that lack nucleoli. Tell: his cells are about three times normal size and the mass is peripheral, the reverse of small cell features.

opts: Brain magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive than computed tomography for brain metastases and is the preferred brain study. Tell: imaging the brain is reasonable; radiating it prophylactically is not recommended with impaired neurocognitive function.

Correct. Prophylactic cranial irradiation is the usual adjuvant step for limited-stage disease after a complete or partial response, but it is not recommended in patients with poor performance status or impaired neurocognitive function. His dementia and dependence in daily activities are both reasons to avoid it.

Computed tomography of the chest and abdomen is part of routine surveillance after small cell treatment. Tell: monitoring scans carry no neurocognitive risk and remain appropriate; it is brain irradiation that is not recommended for him.

Smoking cessation intervention is part of follow-up after small cell treatment. Tell: it is appropriate for anyone, while prophylactic cranial irradiation is the step his impaired cognition argues against.

opts: His age and 45 pack-years fit, but the criteria also require current smoking or quitting within the last 15 years. Tell: he quit 22 years ago, which places him outside the screening window.
ruled out by a stated finding
Pack-years are one criterion; age 55 to 80 and smoking now or within the last 15 years must also be met. Tell: his 45 pack-years pass, but quitting 22 years ago fails the timing rule.
His age is not the problem: the screening range runs from 55 to 80 years, and he is 72. Tell: the criterion he fails is time since quitting, 22 years against a limit of 15.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man has a peripheral cavitating lung mass. Histology shows anaplastic, undifferentiated, pleomorphic cells, with no features of adenocarcinoma or squamous cell carcinoma and no specific marker. He asks how his cancer type was decided. Which response is accurate?
opts: Large cell carcinoma has no specific genetic or histologic marker, which is exactly why it is diagnosed by exclusion. Tell: his report states no specific marker was found, yet the cell type was still named.

Cavitation is seen in several lung cancers, including squamous cell and small cell carcinoma, and a cavitated mass still needs biopsy with histology. Tell: imaging suggests the type, but tissue that excludes the other types decides it.

Sputum testing can catch squamous cell carcinoma, a central bronchial tumor, unlike the other lung cancers. Tell: his mass is peripheral and was typed from histology by excluding adenocarcinoma and squamous features.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion

Correct. Large cell carcinoma lacks specific genetic or histologic markers and is a diagnosis of exclusion among the non-small cell cancers. set2.q: A 58-year-old man has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes a day for 25 years. He plans to keep smoking but cut down to half a pack a day, and he asks whether the amount he smokes each day makes any difference to his lung cancer risk. Which response is accurate?
opts: Halving his packs per day lowers his ongoing exposure, but the 25 years already smoked still count toward a risk that compounds with packs and years. Tell: smoking less is not the same as never having smoked; smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancers.
Packs and years compound the risk

Correct. Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancers, and both the packs smoked per day and the years of smoking compound the risk, raising it 5 times, then 10 times, then 20 times as exposure grows. His daily amount therefore matters, not just how long he has smoked.
Years count, packs per day do not

Duration is only half of his exposure: packs smoked per day and years of smoking compound each other, multiplying the risk from 5 times to 10 times to 20 times. Tell: his daily amount is one of the two factors that multiply his risk, so it does make a difference.

Lung cancer risk keeps rising with exposure rather than locking in: the packs per day and the years of smoking compound the risk as they add up. Tell: each further year of smoking adds to the compounded risk, so how much he smokes from now on still matters.

opts: Correct. Screening is recommended for high-risk adults without symptoms or a known nodule who are 55 to 80 years old, with at least a 30 pack-year history, who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. She is 67, has 2 packs a day x 20 years = 40 pack-years, and quit 8 years ago, so she qualifies for an annual low-dose chest scan.
Quitting does not disqualify her: people who quit within the last 15 years still qualify. Tell: she quit 8 years ago, at 67 years old with 40 pack-years, so she meets every screening criterion.

Sputum cytology is not sensitive and is not the screening test. Tell: eligible patients are screened annually with low-dose chest computed tomography, which works because air and nodules contrast sharply.

Screening uses a lower radiation dose than a standard chest scan to reduce radiation exposure, which works because lung tissue gives high contrast between air and nodules. Tell: the screening study is the low-dose scan, not a standard-dose one.

set2.q: A 71-year-old man with a 60 pack-year history has 2 months of cough, wheezing and blood-streaked sputum. Computed tomography shows a central mass arising in the right main bronchus, and sputum cytology shows malignant cells. Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Small cell carcinoma is also central, but it infiltrates the mucosa and is usually metastatic by the time of diagnosis. Tell: catching the tumor on sputum cytology is the feature of squamous cell carcinoma, the central bronchial tumor diagnosable from sputum.

Adenocarcinoma usually forms in the mid-lung and periphery, often near peripheral scars, and is not amenable to early detection. Tell: his mass is central in a main bronchus and shed malignant cells into his sputum.

Large cell carcinoma forms in the periphery as a large cavitated mass and spreads to unusual sites such as the bowel. Tell: a central bronchial mass caught on sputum cytology points to squamous cell carcinoma instead.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma sits centrally and often originates in a bronchus, has the strongest association with smoking, and causes cough, wheezing and hemoptysis once it obstructs the bronchus. Unlike the other lung cancers it can be caught with sputum testing, so malignant cells in his sputum from a central bronchial mass point to it.

opts: Stage 2B with a small tumor allows spread only to peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes. Tell: his nodes are mediastinal and subcarinal, N2, which pushes any cancer into stage 3.

Correct. Mediastinal or subcarinal node involvement (N2) automatically moves a cancer to stage 3, and a tumor no more than 5 cm that has spread to the mediastinal and subcarinal nodes is stage 3A. His tumor is only 2.5 cm, but the same-side mediastinal nodes set the stage.

Stage 3B with a tumor of 5 cm or less needs mediastinal or hilar nodes on the side without the tumor, or supraclavicular or scalene nodes. Tell: his nodes are on the same side as a 2.5-cm tumor, which is stage 3A.

Stage 4A needs spread to the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, the fluid around the lungs or heart, or one site outside the chest. Tell: he has no distant metastasis, and every stage 1 to 3 cancer is M0.

set2.q: A 47-year-old woman has months of episodes of skin flushing, watery diarrhea with cramps, and wheezing. Exam shows an enlarged liver and a heart murmur, and echocardiography shows thickening of the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. Computed tomography shows a mass in a bronchus. Which tumor is most likely?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma is a central bronchial tumor whose particular paraneoplastic finding is hypercalcemia. Tell: flushing with diarrhea and tricuspid and pulmonic valve thickening is carcinoid syndrome from serotonin.

Adenocarcinoma is usually peripheral, with cough and shortness of breath early and bone pain and weight loss later. Tell: episodic flushing, diarrhea and right-sided valve disease are the serotonin picture of a bronchial carcinoid.

Correct. Carcinoid syndrome, which in the lung arises mainly from a bronchial carcinoid, comes from release of serotonin by the tumor cells. Its features include cutaneous flushes, diarrhea, cramps, nausea and vomiting, cough, wheezing and dyspnea, hepatomegaly, and pulmonic and tricuspid valve thickening and stenosis, matching her picture.

Small cell carcinoma has neuroendocrine paraneoplastic effects, but its classic syndrome is inappropriate antidiuretic hormone with low sodium and confusion. Tell: flushing, diarrhea and right-sided valve thickening are serotonin effects of carcinoid syndrome.

set2.q: A 58-year-old woman has a peripheral lung adenocarcinoma resected. The pathology report describes lepidic growth (tumor cells spreading along the alveolar lining). She asks which lung cells this cancer usually starts from. Which response is accurate?
opts: Type I pneumocytes are thin, squamous cells covering about 95% of the alveolar surface and carrying out gas exchange. Tell: adenocarcinoma arises from the other alveolar cell, the surfactant-secreting type II pneumocyte.

Neuroendocrine cells line the bronchioles and are tied to small cell carcinoma and its paraneoplastic syndromes. Tell: lepidic growth along the alveolar lining traces back to type II pneumocytes, the usual origin of adenocarcinoma.

Squamous cell carcinoma is the type that often originates in the bronchus, centrally. Tell: her tumor is peripheral with lepidic growth along the alveolar lining, which points to type II pneumocytes, the usual origin of adenocarcinoma.

Correct. Type II pneumocytes are usually the origin of adenocarcinomas, starting with atypical adenomatous hyperplasia and growing first in situ, then enlarging by lepidic growth across the alveolar lining or invading the stroma. Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal, secrete surfactant and make up 60% of alveolar epithelial cells but only 3 to 5% of the surface.

Computed tomography shows a central mass in a main bronchus with cavitation and a spiculated (spiky) border. Which noninvasive test can sometimes catch this tumor type, unlike the other lung cancers?
opts: Correct. A central, cavitating bronchial mass in a heavy smoker with cough, wheezing and hemoptysis is the picture of squamous cell carcinoma, which unlike the other lung cancers can be caught with sputum testing. Sputum cytology is not sensitive in general, so tissue biopsy is still the standard.

A serum calcium can show hypercalcemia, a paraneoplastic finding seen particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, but it does not identify the tumor. Tell: the noninvasive test that can catch the tumor cells themselves is sputum cytology.

A mucicarmine stain is done on biopsy tissue and shows mucin production, which relates to adenocarcinoma. Tell: it needs tissue, so it is not noninvasive, and mucin points to a peripheral tumor rather than a central bronchial one.

A chest film is not a good tool for working up a suspicious nodule or symptoms. Tell: computed tomography has already shown the mass, and of the lung cancers it is squamous cell carcinoma that can be caught with sputum.

set2.q: A 66-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed lung cancer is meeting a radiation oncologist. Her son has read that some lung cancers respond far better to radiotherapy than others, and he asks which type benefits most. Which response is accurate?
opts: Correct. Small cell carcinoma responds better to chemotherapy and radiation than the three non-small cell cancers, and radiation works best when it is in limited stage. Non-small cell cancers do not respond well to chemotherapy or radiation, which serve as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4.

Adenocarcinoma is a non-small cell cancer, and these respond poorly to chemotherapy and radiation, which are adjuncts to surgical resection. Tell: the cancer that responds better to radiation is small cell carcinoma.

Large cell carcinoma has no standardized treatment because of its variety and rarity, and as a non-small cell type it responds poorly to radiation. Tell: radiotherapy benefits small cell carcinoma most, especially in limited stage.

Squamous cell carcinoma is a non-small cell cancer, and these do not respond well to chemotherapy or radiation, which serve as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4. Tell: the type singled out for a better response is small cell carcinoma.

opts: There is no 5-year screening interval: eligible people are screened annually with low-dose chest computed tomography. Tell: she is not eligible at all, because the age range stops at 80.

Correct. Screening is recommended for adults 55 to 80 with at least a 30 pack-year history who smoke now or quit within the last 15 years. Her 60 pack-years and current smoking would qualify, but at 83 she is beyond the upper age limit of 80.
Current smoking and 60 pack-years meet two criteria, but the age range ends at 80. Tell: at 83 she falls outside the screening window despite her heavy smoking.
ruled out by a stated finding
Smoking now does not disqualify anyone: the criteria include current smokers and those who quit within the last 15 years. Tell: her age, 83, is what places her outside the range.

set2.q: A 62-year-old man with a 50 pack-year history and no cough or shortness of breath comes to the emergency department after a first seizure. He reports 3 weeks of morning headaches, vomiting and blurred vision, and fundoscopic exam shows papilledema. Chest computed tomography shows a 4-cm lung mass. Which site of spread is most likely?
opts: Correct. Patients may have no respiratory symptoms and present instead with complaints from metastasis. Brain metastasis causes headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncope and seizures, and raised intracranial pressure shows as papilledema on fundoscopic exam, which is his exact picture beside a lung mass.

Liver metastasis causes a dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, poor appetite, jaundice and hepatic failure. Tell: seizures, headaches, blurred vision and papilledema are neurologic findings from raised intracranial pressure, not hepatic ones.

Bone metastasis causes bone pain, fractures without falls and spinal cord compression. Tell: his findings center on raised intracranial pressure, with papilledema, headache and vomiting, which places the spread inside the skull.

Adrenal spread causes adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Tell: a seizure with papilledema and morning headaches signals a brain lesion, not hormone loss.

set2.q: A 45-year-old woman who has never smoked and has no family history of lung cancer has a solitary 4-mm solid nodule found on computed tomography done for abdominal pain. She asks whether she should be worried about it. Which response is accurate?
opts: A biopsy is not the step for a nodule this small in a low-risk patient: anything smaller than 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is at high risk. Tell: biopsy belongs to concerning nodules, such as those with intense uptake or a high probability of malignancy.

Size is the first thing assessed, and 6 mm is the threshold: smaller nodules are generally not concerning, while nodules greater than 6 mm raise concern. Tell: her 4-mm nodule sits below that line in a patient without risk factors.

Correct. The first evaluation of a nodule is its size, and anything smaller than 6 mm is generally not concerning unless the patient is at high risk. Most nodules are benign, mainly granulomas or hamartomas. She has no smoking or family history, so her 4-mm nodule falls in the low-concern group.

Most lung nodules are benign, mainly granulomas (inflammatory) or hamartomas (connective tissue growth). Tell: concern rises with size above 6 mm, upper lobe or hilar location, a spiky border or a high-risk patient, and her nodule has none of these.

set2.q: A 67-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history has a mass arising in a bronchus, and the biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. His oncologist explains that lung carcinomas are sorted into two main groups that are treated differently. Into which group does his cancer fall?
opts: Correct. Lung carcinomas fall into two main types: small cell lung carcinoma (oat cell) and non-small cell lung carcinoma, which is subdivided by histology into adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma. His squamous cell carcinoma therefore belongs to the non-small cell group.

Small cell lung carcinoma, also called oat cell carcinoma, is the other main group, with small, fragile cells that lack nucleoli. Tell: squamous cell carcinoma is one of the three histologic subtypes of the non-small cell group, not part of small cell disease.

Carcinoid tumors are listed among the mixed and rare types, apart from the two main groups, and in the lung they cause carcinoid syndrome from a bronchial carcinoid. Tell: his biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma, a main non-small cell subtype.

Adenosquamous carcinoma is a mixed type that combines two histologies. Tell: his biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma alone, with no glandular component described, so it is classed simply as non-small cell lung carcinoma.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man with known metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma has 3 weeks of fatigue, weight loss and dizziness. His blood pressure is 88/56 mm Hg, serum sodium 128 mEq/L (normal 135-145) and serum potassium 5.9 mEq/L (normal 3.5-5.0). Which complication best explains these findings?
opts: Brain metastasis presents with headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncope or seizures, and papilledema when intracranial pressure rises. Tell: none of those are described, and brain spread would not produce his hyperkalemia and low blood pressure.

Liver metastasis causes a dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, poor appetite, jaundice and eventually hepatic failure. Tell: his picture is hypotension with low sodium and high potassium, the electrolyte pattern of adrenal insufficiency.

Correct. Metastatic spread can cause adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension and electrolyte imbalances: hyponatremia together with hyperkalemia. His low blood pressure, sodium of 128 against a floor of 135, and potassium of 5.9 against a ceiling of 5.0 complete that picture.

The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, typically from small cell carcinoma, retains water and lowers sodium and serum osmolality, causing confusion, seizures and ataxia. Tell: it does not explain his high potassium and hypotension, which point to adrenal insufficiency.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man has a biopsy-proven 3-cm adenocarcinoma in the left lower lobe and a new left pleural effusion. Analysis of the fluid shows malignant cells. There is no spread outside the chest. Which stage is his cancer?
opts: Stage 2B covers tumors of more than 5 cm up to 7 cm without nodes, or smaller tumors with hilar node spread, all without metastasis. Tell: malignant cells in his pleural fluid are distant metastasis, and every stage 1 to 3 cancer is M0.

Stage 3B rests on node spread, to supraclavicular or scalene nodes or the far side's mediastinal or hilar nodes, or same-side mediastinal nodes with a larger tumor, and has no metastasis. Tell: a malignant effusion is M1a, which leaves stage 3 behind.

Correct. A malignant pleural effusion is scored M1a, distant metastasis, along with a tumor in the other lung or a pleural or pericardial nodule. Stage 4A covers spread into the other lung, the lung's lining, the heart's lining or the fluid around the lungs or heart, or a single site outside the chest. His malignant effusion makes him stage 4A whatever the tumor size.
Stage 4B is spread to multiple sites outside the chest, such as the adrenal gland and bones. Tell: his spread is into the pleural fluid within the chest, with nothing outside it, which is stage 4A.

set2.q: A 60-year-old man with a 40 pack-year history has a concerning 2-cm peripheral nodule on computed tomography. He is afraid of needles and asks whether a sputum test could rule out cancer instead of a biopsy. Which response is accurate?
opts: A negative result rules it out

A negative sputum test cannot rule out cancer, because sputum cytology is not sensitive. Tell: the reliable answer comes from tissue, obtained by bronchoscopy, a transthoracic approach or thoracoscopy depending on the nodule's location.
It works best for peripheral tumors

Sputum testing catches central bronchial tumors, mainly squamous cell carcinoma, not peripheral ones. Tell: adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma sit in the periphery and are not amenable to early detection, so a peripheral nodule is the worst case for sputum.

Staging uses computed tomography for location and size, positron emission tomography for lymph involvement and biopsy for tumor type. Tell: sputum cytology plays no part in staging, and it is not sensitive enough even for diagnosis.

Correct. Sputum cytology is listed in the workup but is not sensitive, so a negative result cannot rule out cancer. It is mainly useful for squamous cell carcinoma, a central bronchial tumor that can be caught with sputum testing, while peripheral tumors such as adenocarcinoma and large cell carcinoma are not. Biopsy classes the tumor type.

set2.q: A 65-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma diagnosed 6 months ago has sudden, severe mid-back pain that began during a coughing fit. She has not fallen. Imaging shows a fresh vertebral fracture. Which complication best explains the fracture?
opts: Liver metastasis brings a dull right upper quadrant ache, firm hepatomegaly, poor appetite and jaundice. Tell: a spinal fracture after a cough with no fall points to bone weakened by metastasis, not liver involvement.

Adrenal involvement causes adrenal insufficiency: fatigue, weight loss, dizziness, hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Tell: none of that explains a vertebral fracture from coughing, which reflects bone metastasis.

Correct. Lung cancer spreads to bone, which can be anywhere, including the spine. Bone metastasis causes bone pain, fractures without a fall, even a spinal fracture from coughing, and spinal cord compression with neurologic dysfunction. A vertebral fracture from a cough in a patient with lung adenocarcinoma fits exactly.

Brain metastasis presents with headaches, vision changes, nausea, vomiting, syncope or seizures. Tell: her complaint is back pain and a vertebral fracture from coughing, which is the bone picture, not a brain one.

set2.q: A 68-year-old man who still smokes and has a 70 pack-year history has 2 months of cough, wheezing and hemoptysis. Computed tomography shows a large, cavitated central mass arising from a bronchus. A metabolic panel shows a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5). Which lung cancer type is most likely?
opts: Adenocarcinoma usually forms in the mid-lung and periphery, often near scars. Tell: his tumor is central and bronchial, with hypercalcemia, the pattern of squamous cell carcinoma.

Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma has the strongest association with smoking, sits centrally and often originates in a bronchus, cavitates frequently, and causes cough, wheezing and hemoptysis once it obstructs the airway. Hypercalcemia is a paraneoplastic finding seen particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, and his calcium of 12.8 exceeds the 10.5 ceiling.

Small cell carcinoma is also central and can cavitate once large, but its classic paraneoplastic picture is low sodium from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone, not high calcium. Tell: hypercalcemia with a central cavitated bronchial mass points to squamous cell carcinoma.

Large cell carcinoma also forms a large cavitated mass, but in the periphery, not arising from a bronchus. Tell: cavitation alone does not decide the type; the central bronchial origin and hypercalcemia point to squamous cell carcinoma.

opts: Discharge treats one negative biopsy as proof, but a biopsy can miss the tumor. Tell: his nodule is spiky, in the upper lobe and enlarging, all concerning features, and a feared false negative leads to repeat biopsy or excision.

Screening is for high-risk people without symptoms or a known nodule. Tell: he already has an enlarging, spiky nodule with a possibly false-negative biopsy, so the next move is repeat biopsy or excision.

Chemotherapy without a confirmed cancer or a stage skips the diagnosis entirely, and for non-small cell cancer it is an adjunct or stage 4 therapy. Tell: no malignancy has been proven yet, so tissue must come first, by repeat biopsy or excision.

Correct. When an image-guided biopsy does not confirm malignancy, the pathway is to consider a repeat biopsy or to proceed to excision if there is concern about a false-negative biopsy. His spiky border, upper-lobe location and growth over time are all concerning features, so a negative result does not end the workup.

set2.q: A 70-year-old man had chest radiotherapy for small cell lung carcinoma 4 years ago and remains free of cancer. He now has progressive exertional dyspnea, and computed tomography shows scarring confined to the treated area of lung. Which late effect of radiotherapy explains his symptoms?
opts: Lymphedema and fluid retention follow damage to the lymphatic system, classically in the axilla. Tell: they cause limb swelling, not scarring of the treated lung with exertional dyspnea.
Neuropathy is a chronic effect of radiotherapy on nerves. Tell: nerve damage would not show as scarring on lung imaging; his findings point to pulmonary fibrosis in the radiation field.

Correct. Chronic effects of lung radiotherapy include pulmonary fibrosis and scarring of the affected tissues, as well as cardiovascular fibrosis, lymphedema and neuropathy. Scarring limited to the treated area years after radiation, with progressive exertional dyspnea, is radiation pulmonary fibrosis.

Erythema and hyperpigmentation of the skin are acute, localized effects during treatment. Tell: his problem began years later and lies in the lung, with scarring in the treated area, a chronic effect.

set2.q: A 63-year-old woman with a 35 pack-year history has a 9-mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe found on computed tomography for abdominal pain. Which additional feature of the nodule would most raise concern for malignancy?
opts: Popcorn-looking calcification points to a hamartoma, a benign connective tissue growth. Tell: it is a benign pattern, so it would lower concern; the concerning border is spiky or lobulated.
Fatty tissue inside a nodule points to a hamartoma and is a benign feature. Tell: fat reassures rather than alarms, while a spiculated border is a classic sign of a concerning nodule.

Central calcification is a benign pattern, typical of a healed granuloma. Tell: malignant calcification patterns are eccentric or stippled ground-glass, and a spiky border is the feature that raises concern most here.

Correct. Concerning nodules are greater than 6 mm, sit in the upper lobes or hilar structures, have a spiculated appearance (spikes, deviations or lobulations in the border), number more than 3, enlarge over time, enhance with contrast, appear cavitated or nonsolid, or occur in high-risk patients. A spiky border would add to her size, location and smoking.

set2.q: A 70-year-old woman with known small cell lung carcinoma has a serum sodium of 124 mEq/L (normal 135-145) and low serum osmolality from the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone. Her family asks why her legs and lungs show no swelling if her body is holding on to too much water. Which response is accurate?
opts: Her sodium is 124, well below the normal floor of 135, and her osmolality is low. Tell: water retention dilutes the sodium; the lack of edema comes from the insidious course, not from a high sodium.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. In small cell lung cancer, neuroendocrine tumor cells produce excess antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin), and the body retains too much water, lowering serum sodium and osmolality. The result is confusion, seizures, ataxia and other neurologic dysfunction, but no signs of peripheral or pulmonary edema, because the process is insidious over time.

Her low sodium and low osmolality come from retaining too much water under excess antidiuretic hormone, the opposite of dehydration. Tell: the absence of edema reflects the slow, insidious course, not a fluid deficit.

Edema is not part of this picture: the syndrome produces neurologic dysfunction without peripheral or pulmonary edema, because it develops insidiously. Tell: watch instead for confusion, seizures and ataxia as the sodium falls.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with a 45 pack-year smoking history has a newly diagnosed squamous cell carcinoma forming a mass near the right hilum, with spread to the regional lymph nodes. He asks where the cancer is expected to spread outside the chest. Which sites are expected?
opts: Correct. Lung cancer proliferates locally, spreads to regional lymph nodes and then to distant organs, named as the liver, brain and bone, as angiogenesis lets it exceed its boundaries. Each site can announce itself without a respiratory symptom: a right upper quadrant ache, headaches or seizures, bone pain or fractures.

The small intestine and bowel are unusual metastatic sites characteristic of large cell carcinoma, a peripheral tumor. Tell: his tumor is a hilar squamous cell carcinoma, so its expected distant sites are the usual ones for lung cancer: liver, brain and bone.

Invasion of the heart or great vessels is local growth that classes the primary tumor as T4, not distant metastasis to another organ. Tell: the question asks about spread outside the chest, and distant lung cancer metastases go to the liver, brain and bone.

Scalene and supraclavicular nodes are lymph node involvement, scored N3, which moves the cancer to stage 3 but is not organ metastasis. Tell: after the regional nodes, lung cancer seeds distant organs, named as the liver, brain and bone.

opts: Genetics is one listed risk factor among several, beside radiation and radon, air pollution, toxins, infections, diet and alcohol. Tell: nothing in her history points to an inherited cause, while 30 years of radon exposure is documented.
Radon exposure is a risk factor

Correct. Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of lung cancers, not all of them, and radiation and radon exposure are listed among the other risk factors, beside air pollution, environmental and chemical toxins, tuberculosis or human immunodeficiency virus infection, genetics, diet and alcohol. Her 30 years of radon exposure is a recognized cause.

Smoking is implicated in 85 to 90% of cases, which leaves a share of lung cancers in people who never smoked. Tell: radon, radiation, air pollution, chemical toxins and genetics are all listed risk factors beyond tobacco, and she has a long radon exposure.

Second-hand smoke is a recognized contributor, but she reports no exposure to other people's smoke or any other exposure besides radon. Tell: the exposure actually documented in her history is radon in her home, a listed risk factor in its own right.

opts: Standard stage evaluation, with or without fludeoxyglucose positron emission tomography, is the branch for a high probability of malignancy. Tell: her probability was judged very low, so she enters surveillance rather than staging.

Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with resection is reserved for a high probability without metastases, or for moderate or intense uptake on positron emission tomography. Tell: a very low probability nodule is watched with serial scans, not removed.

Correct. For a new solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm, the first move is to judge the clinical probability of malignancy. A very low probability leads to computed tomography surveillance at 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 24 months, using low-dose, thin-section, noncontrast scans, rather than staging, biopsy or resection.

Dropping follow-up does not fit a solid nodule of 8 to 30 mm, even at very low probability: the pathway still tracks it with surveillance scans out to 18 to 24 months. Tell: a nodule of this size is followed with serial low-dose computed tomography, not dismissed.

opts: This reverses the rule: a nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign. Tell: concerning locations are the upper lobes or hilar structures, and an opacity along the minor fissure is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue.

Resection is reserved for nodules with a high probability of malignancy or intense uptake on positron emission tomography. Tell: an opacity hugging the minor fissure in a never-smoker is a typical benign finding.

A hamartoma is a smoothly marginated solid nodule with internal fat and popcorn calcification. Tell: a flat opacity lying along the minor fissure, with no fat or calcification described, is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue.

Correct. A nodule close to a fissure usually indicates something benign, and a nodular opacity adjacent to the minor fissure is typical of a linear scar or lymphoid tissue. She is a never-smoker without other risk factors, which also lowers concern.

opts: A comprehensive metabolic panel including calcium belongs to the laboratory workup, along with a complete blood count with differential and alkaline phosphatase. Tell: calcium matters because hypercalcemia occurs particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, so this test is useful.

Correct. A chest film is not a good tool for working up a suspicious nodule or symptoms: it may be the first image to show a nodule, but otherwise it serves to rule out other pathology. Her symptoms and opacity call for computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen, then biopsy, with laboratory studies.

Computed tomography with contrast of the chest and upper abdomen is the standard study for a suspicious nodule or symptoms, followed by biopsy or intervention. Tell: this is the scan her workup needs most, the opposite of the least useful study.

Tissue is obtained by bronchoscopy, a transthoracic approach or thoracoscopy depending on the nodule's location, and it can be guided by computed tomography. Tell: biopsy classes the tumor type and is a core part of her workup, not something to skip.

opts: Stage 2B with a small tumor allows spread only to peribronchial, hilar or intrapulmonary nodes on the same side. Tell: a supraclavicular node is N3, and N2 or N3 involvement automatically moves a cancer to stage 3.
Stage 3A with a small tumor means spread to the same-side mediastinal or subcarinal nodes. Tell: a supraclavicular node reaches farther, N3, which places a tumor of 5 cm or less in stage 3B.

Correct. Spread to any supraclavicular or scalene node is N3, which moves a cancer to stage 3. With a tumor no more than 5 cm, spread to supraclavicular or scalene nodes, or to mediastinal or hilar nodes on the side without the tumor, is stage 3B. Her 2-cm tumor with a positive supraclavicular node fits.

Stage 4A is spread to the other lung, the pleura or pericardium, the fluid around the lungs or heart, or one site outside the chest. Tell: a supraclavicular node counts as lymph node involvement, not distant metastasis, and no other organ is involved.

set2.q: A 66-year-old man with a 3.5-cm non-small cell lung carcinoma, no lymph node involvement and no metastasis (stage 1B) is fit for surgery. He would prefer to avoid an operation and asks for chemotherapy and radiation instead. Which plan should be avoided as his primary treatment?
opts: Correct. Stage 1 non-small cell lung cancer is treated with surgical resection when the patient can tolerate it, and chemotherapy and radiation serve only as adjuncts to surgery or for stage 4, because non-small cell cancers respond poorly to them. For a fit patient with stage 1B disease, replacing surgery with chemoradiation gives up the standard treatment.
Lobectomy, removing the entire lobe, is one of the standard resections for stage 1 disease in a patient who can tolerate surgery. Tell: he is fit, so this is the treatment to pursue, not to avoid.

Wedge or segment resection, removing a smaller or larger portion of the lobe, is a standard resection chosen by size and lymph involvement. Tell: resection is the recommended treatment for his stage, so it is appropriate.

Pulmonary function tests are part of the workup, and a patient must be able to tolerate surgery, surviving and recovering from it. Tell: checking his lung function before resection supports the standard plan rather than conflicting with it.
